This document recounts the war between the Achaeans and Trojans, centered on Achilles’ wrath and its consequences. It begins when Agamemnon dishonors Chryses, bringing Apollo’s plague, then takes Briseis from Achilles. Achilles withdraws and asks Thetis to win Jove’s support for the Trojans, while Agamemnon is deceived into expecting victory. After failed efforts to settle the conflict through Menelaus and Alexandrus’s duel, Pandarus breaks the oath, and full war resumes. The Achaeans and Trojans suffer long, shifting battles under frequent divine intervention. Diomed wounds Venus and Mars; Hector proves Troy’s chief defender; and Achilles remains apart despite the Achaeans’ worsening danger. Agamemnon’s embassy, Ulysses, Phoenix, and Ajax, cannot persuade Achilles to accept gifts and return. Trojan attacks eventually breach the Achaean wall and threaten the ships. Jove favors Hector, though Juno, Minerva, and Neptune at times secretly aid the Achaeans. With the ships burning, Patroclus gains Achilles’ permission to lead the Myrmidons in Achilles’ armor. He saves the fleet, kills Sarpedon, but ignores Achilles’ warning to stop at the ships. Apollo, Euphorbus, and Hector bring about Patroclus’ death. A prolonged struggle follows over his body, which Menelaus, Ajax, and others finally recover. Patroclus’s death transforms Achilles. Thetis obtains divine armor from Vulcan, Achilles reconciles with Agamemnon, and he returns to battle despite knowing his own death is near. He devastates the Trojans, fights through the river Xanthus, and finally kills Hector outside Ilius after Minerva deceives Hector. Achilles dishonors Hector’s corpse while Troy mourns. Achilles then holds Patroclus’s funeral, including burning offerings, burial, and athletic games. In the ending, Jove directs Priam to ransom Hector’s body. Priam reaches Achilles with Mercury’s help and appeals to their shared grief. Achilles relents, returns Hector, and grants time for burial. The Trojans lament Hector, burn his body, place his bones in a golden urn, and raise a barrow.

Achilles is a great, mighty mortal hero and Achaean warrior, son of Peleus and Thetis, descendant of Aeacus, king and commander of the Myrmidons. He is the Achaeans’ foremost fighter, possesses immortal horses and exceptional weapons, and is protected and honored by gods, yet is doomed to a short life and to die at Troy after Hector. The central course of his story begins when Agamemnon dishonours him by taking Briseis, his awarded prize. Furious but restrained from attacking Agamemnon, Achilles withdraws from the Trojan War, keeps his Myrmidons from battle, rejects gifts and reconciliation, and asks through Thetis that Jove favor the Trojans. While the Achaeans suffer, he remains at his ships with Patroclus, playing his lyre and refusing to fight. He allows Patroclus to wear his armour and lead the Myrmidons, praying for his victory and safe return, but Patroclus is killed and Hector takes Achilles’ armour. Grief replaces his anger toward Agamemnon. Though he knows his own death will follow Hector’s, Achilles reconciles with Agamemnon, receives armour made by Vulcan, and returns to battle seeking revenge. He kills many Trojans, drives them toward Ilius, and finally kills Hector in single combat. His grief and vengeance continue after the killing: he dishonours Hector’s corpse, drags it behind his chariot, and honors Patroclus with mourning, sacrifice, burial, and funeral games. At Jove’s command, conveyed through Thetis, he accepts Priam’s ransom, cleans and returns Hector’s body, comforts Priam, and restrains war for Hector’s funeral rites. The record ends with Achilles still mourning Patroclus while yielding Hector to his father.

Agamemnon is a king of men, son of Atreus, elder and more powerful brother of Menelaus, husband of Clytemnestra, and father of Chrysothemis, Laodice, Iphianassa, and Orestes. As chief ruler and greatest king of the Achaeans, he commands their largest force, including one hundred ships from Mycenae and associated lands, and leads them in the war against Troy. He is depicted as imposing among heroes and as a commander who honors Nestor, favors Idomeneus, addresses assemblies, directs sacrifices and oaths, organizes battle, and at times personally fights fiercely. The central conflict of his record begins when he refuses Chryses’s ransom and keeps Chryseis, bringing Apollo’s plague on the Achaeans. Though he returns her, he demands compensation and takes Briseis from Achilles. This dishonors Achilles, causes their quarrel, and harms the Achaeans. Agamemnon repeatedly shows forceful, sometimes harsh authority: he urges no mercy for Trojans, kills Adrestus, rebukes hesitant fighters, and seeks the destruction of Priam’s palace and Hector’s death. His leadership also includes fear, uncertainty, and concern for his people. He receives a lying dream, tests the army by proposing departure, later despairs and urges retreat as the Trojans gain strength, and loses sleep over danger to the Achaeans and their ships. Yet he consults other leaders, accepts rebuke, encourages the ranks, and fights until Coon wounds him severely enough to force his withdrawal. After Nestor reproves him, Agamemnon admits wrongdoing and offers extensive gifts and honors to Achilles. Achilles first refuses, while the consequences of Agamemnon’s taking Briseis continue to burden the Achaeans. In the end Agamemnon reconciles with Achilles, attributes his madness to Jove, Fate, and Erinys, restores the promised gifts, swears he did not violate Briseis, and joins the renewed preparation for battle. His final record shows him accepting Achilles’s recognition of his superiority in the javelin contest and assigning the spear to Meriones.

The Achaeans are a Greek army, also called Argives and Danaans, led chiefly by Agamemnon son of Atreus. They besiege Troy for nine years before the tenth, wage war against the Trojans over Helen, and possess a fleet, ships, tents, chariots, and a shore-side camp protected by a wall, gates, trench, and stakes. Their story begins with the sack of Thebe, division of spoil, and Apollo’s deadly pestilence. They return Chryseis, purify themselves, and sacrifice, but a quarrel among their leaders causes Achilles to refuse fighting. Though they initially rush toward their ships when return is proposed, they are recalled to the war, gather in force, make and trust oaths with the Trojans, and repeatedly fight, gain ground, and suffer reverses. As Trojan pressure grows, the Achaeans build defenses around their ships, maintain watches, inspect their guards, and send Ulysses and Diomed to gather intelligence. Their leaders are wounded, they are driven through wall and trench toward the ships, and their army is repeatedly frightened, routed, or forced into desperate defense. Encouragement from figures including Discord, Neptune, Ajax, Nestor, and Idomeneus helps them resist. Patroclus leads the Myrmidons to recover ground, but dies; the Achaeans fight fiercely over bodies including Sarpedon’s and Patroclus’s, eventually recover Patroclus, and mourn him. Achilles’ return changes the battle: the Achaeans arm, press the Trojans back toward Troy, nearly take its gates, and defeat Hector. They strip and carry Hector’s body to their ships. They then mourn and bury Patroclus, hold funeral contests, and remain encamped beside the ships. At the end, Priam secretly crosses their camp for Hector’s body, and Achilles promises they will not attack Troy during the agreed mourning and funeral period.

The Trojans are the warrior people and army of Troy and Ilius, living there with their wives, little ones, Priam, and his people. Led chiefly by Hector and joined by allies from many places, including the Dardanians, they speak diverse languages and defend Troy for their families in war with the Achaeans over Helen. They hate Alexandrus for the danger he has caused, yet after Pandarus breaks the oaths by attacking Menelaus, they renew the war. They suffer reverses early but are repeatedly rallied by Hector, Apollo, Mars, Aeneas, and their allies. Jove’s promised aid gives them a major advantage: they drive the Achaeans through the trench, camp by the ships with watchfires and sentinels, breach the wall, and assault the fleet, seeking to burn it. Their strength fluctuates through fierce fighting at the ships, around fallen warriors, and over Patroclus’s body. They are at times routed, yet press to take Patroclus to Ilius and confine the Achaeans at their ships. Their advance ends when Achilles returns. Patroclus first drives them back, though Apollo helps Hector kill him; then Achilles defeats and pursues them across the plain and in Xanthus. They flee in panic into Ilius under Apollo’s protection. Hector remains outside as Troy’s chief defender and is killed by Achilles, leaving the city endangered. The Trojans mourn him throughout the city, then receive his body, burn it, gather his bones in a golden urn, raise a burial mound, and hold a feast in Priam’s house.

Apollo is an immortal god, son of Jove/Zeus and Leto, lord of the silver bow and Far-Darter. He acts chiefly through divine force in the conflict between Achaeans and Trojans, serving Jove while repeatedly aiding Troy, Ilius, Hector, and Aeneas. When Agamemnon dishonors his priest Chryses, Apollo hears the priest’s prayer and sends a deadly pestilence among the Achaeans; it ends only after Chryseis is returned and sacrifice is made at Chryse. He rescues Aeneas from Diomed, hides him in darkness, takes him to Pergamus for healing by Latona and Diana, and creates a likeness of him to sustain the battle. He helps shape fighting through counsel, disguises, healing, and direct intervention: raising Hector, restoring his strength, carrying Jove’s aegis to panic the Achaeans, advancing the Trojans, and destroying the Achaean wall. He heals Glaucus and transports Sarpedon’s cleansed body to Lycia. He prevents Patroclus from taking Troy and helps make Hector’s attack on Patroclus possible. Later he incites Hector and Aeneas, strengthens Aeneas against Achilles, warns Hector against single combat, protects Hector in darkness, and defends Ilius by drawing Achilles away from its people. Yet his protection has a limit: after sustaining Hector during the pursuit, Apollo leaves when Hector’s doom is weighed, and Hector can no longer escape.

Chryses is a priest of Apollo and father of Chryseis. He comes to the Achaean ships with Apollo’s sceptre and ransom to seek her release, but Agamemnon rejects and insults him. Chryses prays for vengeance; later Ulysses returns Chryseis to him, and he leads sacrifice and prayer that end the pestilence.

Chryseis, daughter of Chryses, is awarded to Agamemnon as spoil from Thebe and held after he rejects her father’s ransom. To appease Apollo, Agamemnon releases her without payment; Ulysses returns her to Chryse, where Chryses gladly receives her.

Briseis is a captive woman, daughter of Briseus, taken after Achilles sacked Lyrnessus and awarded to Achilles as his prize. Achilles cherishes her, but Agamemnon takes her from his tent through heralds as compensation for surrendering Chryseis, an injury Achilles refuses to forgive. Agamemnon later offers her return and swears he has not had relations with her. Returned among his gifts, Briseis finds Patroclus dead, grieves for him, and recalls his promise that Achilles would marry her and take her to Phthia.

Jove is a god: the supreme, most glorious ruler and king of gods and men, lord of counsel, lightning, thunder, storm-cloud, and heaven. A son of Saturn, he rules Olympus and Mount Ida, sits or watches from Olympus and Ida, possesses the aegis, thunderbolt, and golden scales that weigh fates, and is stronger and older than Neptune. He is husband of Juno and is named father of Apollo, Minerva, Mars, Hercules, Vulcan, Xanthus, Achilles through descent, Hector, and even Saturn. He is invoked as witness and guardian of covenants, prayers, sacrifices, and oaths, yet grants or withholds requests according to his own will. The central course of his action is his promise to Thetis: he will favor the Trojans until the Achaeans honor Achilles. He confirms this promise by bowing his head, then sends a lying dream to Agamemnon, accepts sacrifice without granting Agamemnon’s request, and helps bring about continued fighting. Although he considers peace and is invoked over the covenant, he orders Minerva to cause the Trojans to break their oaths. From Ida, he forbids divine intervention, weighs the battle toward the Trojans, sends thunder, lightning, wind, and portents, strengthens Hector, and drives the Achaeans back. He restrains Juno, Minerva, and Neptune while commanding Iris and Apollo to restore Hector and renew the Trojan attack. His favor is not simple or permanent. He protects Ilius and supports Hector to glorify Achilles, while foreseeing Hector’s death and refusing to destroy the Achaeans completely. He grants Achilles’s prayer that the Achaeans suffer, later pities Achilles, his horses, and Priam, and at times aids the Achaeans by clearing darkness or sending Minerva. Near the end he permits the gods to aid either side, weighs Hector’s doom against Achilles’s, and lets Hector’s doom sink. Finally, he orders that Hector’s body be released, instructs Thetis and Priam through Iris, and promises Priam safe passage to Achilles’s tent.

Juno is a goddess, queen of the goddesses and gods, eldest daughter of Saturn, sister and wife of Jove/Jupiter, and mother of Mars and Vulcan. She possesses a gold-bedizened chariot and favors Argos, Sparta, and Mycenae. Her central concern is the war: she supports the Argives, Achaeans, and Danaans, cares for Achilles and Agamemnon, and is fiercely hostile to the Trojans, Ilius, Priam’s people, and their advance. She repeatedly seeks Troy’s destruction, out of anger and a sworn refusal to protect its people. Her course unfolds through conflict with Jove’s Trojan policy. She suspects Thetis has won Jove’s aid for Achilles, reproaches Jove, fears his threat, and temporarily falls silent. She rejects peace, urges Minerva to make the Trojans break their oaths, drives to Troy to encourage the Argives, and presses Neptune and Minerva to aid the failing Greeks. Though Iris delivers Jove’s command that restrains her from battle, Juno continues to offer the Argives counsel and influence Agamemnon. Determined to change events, she deceives Jupiter: she obtains Venus’s girdle, enlists Sleep, and seduces Jupiter on Mount Ida so Neptune may aid the Achaeans. Later she denies causing Neptune’s intervention, carries Jove’s orders to Iris and Apollo, and warns the gods that his plans will trouble mortals and immortals. She secretly sends Iris to Achilles, sends the sun into Oceanus to provide the Achaeans rest, joins the gods defending Achilles, hinders fleeing Trojans with mist, and directs Vulcan against Xanthus before stopping the violence. Still angry, she celebrates Minerva’s victory over Venus and beats Diana when challenged.

Minerva is a goddess, daughter of aegis-bearing Jove and child of Zeus, marked by her priceless, tasselled aegis and stout spear. A marshaller of hosts and goddess of plunder, she is chiefly aligned with the Achaeans and Danaans in the conflict against Troy, usually aiding through counsel, courage, disguise, and selective intervention rather than open fighting. She serves Juno by preventing the Achaeans’ departure, restores order through Ulysses, urges wavering fighters onward, and descends at Jove’s command to induce the breaking of oaths while protecting Menelaus from a mortal wound. She repeatedly strengthens and befriends Diomed, helps him against Venus and Mars, deflects Mars’s spear, and drives Diomed’s spear into Mars; she later personally strikes down Mars and Venus. She assists Achilles, Menelaus, and Ulysses, protects Achilles with Jove’s sanction, and can terrify Trojans, improve strength or speed, and make an opponent slip. Her power is constrained by Jove: she seeks to act with Juno against the Trojans but withdraws under threat of punishment, remaining furious and plotting mischief. She also cooperates with Apollo to pause a day’s fighting through Hector’s challenge. Near the end, she helps Achilles escape Xanthus, argues that Hector’s death must proceed, then takes Deiphobus’s form and voice to deceive Hector into fighting; she retrieves Achilles’ spear and helps secure Hector’s defeat. Her final recorded act favors Ulysses in a running contest by lightening him and causing Ajax son of Oileus to fall.

Thetis is an immortal, silver-footed marine goddess and sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus, the old sea-god or old merman. She is reared by Juno, saved by Vulcan in his childhood, and married to Peleus against her will. Above all, she is the loving, grieving mother of the mortal Achilles. When Achilles suffers, she rises from the sea to comfort him, seeks Jove’s aid, and persuades him to favor the Trojans until Achilles receives his due. After Patroclus dies, she foretells that Achilles’ death will follow Hector’s, obtains splendid armour from Vulcan, brings it to Achilles, and preserves Patroclus’s body with ambrosia and nectar. Finally, summoned by Jove, she tells Achilles to accept ransom for Hector’s body, and he obeys.

Hector is a mortal Trojan prince, son of Priam and Hecuba, husband of Andromache, father of Astyanax, brother of Paris and other Trojan kin, and Troy’s foremost warrior, commander, guardian, and chief defender. He is valued for courage, counsel, devotion to his people, and determination to protect Ilius, though he knows Troy is fated to fall. He rebukes Paris, organizes the city’s defense, urges prayers and offerings, visits Andromache and their child, and returns to battle rather than avoid his duty. Throughout the war he leads Trojan and allied forces at the front, rallies councils and troops, challenges Ajax to single combat, breaches the Achaean wall, drives toward the ships, and threatens them with fire. Supported at times by Jove and Apollo, he withstands wounds and repeatedly renews the assault. He orders Dolon to spy on the Achaeans, rejects an omen in favor of trusting Jove, and at key moments accepts or refuses Polydamas’s advice. His greatest battlefield success is killing Patroclus with Apollo’s aid, stripping Patroclus of Achilles’ armour, and wearing it in triumph; this makes him Achilles’ central enemy. Apollo warns Hector not to face Achilles alone and at times saves him, but after Patroclus’s death the conflict closes around them. Hector remains outside the gates despite his parents’ pleas, runs three times around the city, and finally faces Achilles after Minerva deceives him in the likeness of Deiphobus. Achilles wounds him in the throat and kills him. Hector asks for his body to be returned, but it is stripped, dragged behind Achilles’ chariot, and dishonoured. Venus and Apollo preserve it from dogs, sun, and decay. Priam ransoms the body; Troy mourns its glory and protector, burns it, buries the bones, and raises a barrow.

Menelaus is a son of Atreus, younger brother and brother-in-law of Agamemnon, husband of Helen, commander of Sparta and neighboring Lacedaemonian settlements, and a Danaan and Achaean warrior. Helen’s removal to Troy is the central injury shaping his actions: he seeks revenge for the toil and sorrow it caused, and the Argives fight for his sake. Though called brave and loud in battle-cry, he is also described as often remiss and unwilling to exert himself. He begins by urging his people to fight and by eagerly meeting Alexandrus in single combat. He pierces Alexandrus’s defenses, breaks his sword, and nearly drags him away before Venus intervenes; Menelaus is declared victor. As champion in the agreement with the Trojans, he is then wounded by Pandarus’s arrow, reassures Agamemnon, and receives treatment from Machaon. He captures Adrestus but is persuaded by Agamemnon not to spare him. He volunteers against Hector after rebuking reluctant Achaeans, but Agamemnon prevents the duel. Menelaus remains anxious for the Argives, helps rouse the camp, aids in rescuing Ulysses, and fights repeatedly: he wounds Helenus, kills Pisander and Dolops, and denounces the Trojans for taking Helen and treasure and attacking the ships. His most sustained effort centers on Patroclus’s body. He stands over it, kills Euphorbus and Podes, seeks Ajax’s help against Hector’s force, sends Antilochus to tell Achilles of Patroclus’s death, and helps defend and carry the body away. At the chariot race, Antilochus forces him aside. Menelaus protests and demands an oath, but when Antilochus yields the mare, Menelaus’s anger ends and he returns it.

Patroclus is a son of Menoetius, an Achaean and Myrmidon warrior, and Achilles’ dearest, trusted companion, attendant, and squire. Though older and less nobly born than Achilles, he serves him closely: he helps prepare a feast, obeys him, and is guided by his father’s charge. His compassion is central as well as his courage. Sent to learn of the wounded, he carries Eurypylus into a tent, removes and dresses his wound, and cares for him until the worsening battle compels him to seek Achilles. Moved by the Achaeans’ suffering, Patroclus weeps and asks to lead the Myrmidons while wearing Achilles’ armour. He drives back the Trojans, helps save the ships, commands the Danaans, and kills many fighters, including Pyraechmes, Pronous, Thestor, Erylaus, and Sarpedon in single combat. Pursuing the retreating Trojans and Lycians, he tries to reach Hector, attacks Troy’s wall, kills Cebriones, and fights over his body. His success ends when Phoebus Apollo overpowers and strikes him, Euphorbus wounds him from behind, and Hector gives the fatal blow. Dying, Patroclus foretells Hector’s death by Achilles. Afterward, his body and Achilles’ armour become the focus of fierce fighting. His death causes profound grief, above all for Achilles, whose vengeance against Hector is driven by the loss of his comrade. Patroclus is mourned by the Myrmidons and Achaeans; his body is preserved, burned on a richly supplied pyre, and his bones are placed in a golden urn beneath a burial mound. Funeral contests honor him. Even after Hector’s body is returned to his father, Achilles speaks to Patroclus and continues to share his grief and honor with him. Patroclus is ultimately buried with Achilles in a single urn.

Nestor is an aged Achaean and Pylian king: son of Neleus, ruler of Pylos and the Pylian people in his third generation of rule, knight of Gerene, warrior, commander, and father of Thrasymedes. Though old age restricts his physical strength and prevents him from boxing or wrestling, his judgment, eloquence, and counsel make him the foremost councillor in Agamemnon’s esteem and a leader whom the Achaeans hear sooner than any other. He commands ninety ships’ worth of Pylian and neighboring forces, rivals Menestheus in marshalling troops, and owns notable possessions including a gold shield and a richly worked cup brought from home. At the outset, he supports arming the Achaeans, advises Agamemnon to organize them by tribes and clans, recalls signs concerning Troy, and presses for prompt action. He arranges the Pylians for battle, instructing charioteers to hold formation and fight with spears rather than separately. He rebukes fear of Hector, invokes his youthful defeat of Ereuthalion, and proposes both a chosen champion and defenses for the ships. When his horse is disabled and Hector threatens him, Diomed rescues him; Nestor then urges retreat when Jove favors Hector. As the crisis deepens, Nestor recommends watchfulness, feasting, counsel, gifts, and conciliatory words to address Agamemnon’s conflict with Achilles. He helps inspect the guards, proposes reconnaissance in the Trojan camp, and warns sentinels against sleep. He also removes and tends the wounded Machaon, reports the wounded leaders to Patroclus, and urges Patroclus to persuade Achilles to send aid. After the wall falls, he joins deliberation among the wounded chiefs and later restores courage by appealing to the Achaeans’ families, property, and honor. At the games, he teaches Antilochus chariot-racing skill and receives an urn from Achilles, recalling earlier victories in boxing, wrestling, running, and spear-throwing, while acknowledging that the sons of Actor surpassed him in chariot races.

Ulysses is an Achaean leader, warrior, counsellor, Ithacan hero, and son of Laertes, father of Telemachus. He commands and leads the Cephallenians, contributing twelve ships, and is repeatedly valued for craft, stratagems, daring, counsel, and Minerva’s favor and protection. At the outset he obeys Agamemnon’s order to return Chryseis and the hecatomb to Chryses. He then keeps the Achaeans together: he refuses to launch his ship, restores order in the assembly, rebukes Thersites, and recalls the prophecy of eventual victory. In battle he promises to fight in the foremost ranks, kills Democoon after Leucus dies, attacks Lycian forces, and later is wounded while resisting Hector’s side before Menelaus and Ajax rescue him. He also flees toward the ships when Diomed calls for help defending Nestor. As an envoy with Phoenix and Ajax, he presents Agamemnon’s offers to Achilles, urges him to save the Achaeans, and reports Achilles’ refusal. During the night reconnaissance, he accompanies Diomed, helps intercept and question Dolon, learns the enemy dispositions, honors Minerva, and helps seize Rhesus’s horses. He strongly opposes withdrawing the ships, advises Achilles that the Achaeans must eat and arm before battle, and presses Agamemnon to swear concerning Briseis. The records end with his athletic cunning: he wrestles Ajax and wins the running contest after praying to Minerva.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad
s: Ajax son of Telamon is an Achaean warrior, champion, leader, captain, envoy, and great wrestler: a foremost defender whose stature and prowess rank him immediately after Achilles while Achilles remains apart. He brings twelve ships from Salamis, stations them beside the Athenians, and commands a large body of foot soldiers. His broad, mighty, sevenfold ox-hide shield, faced with bronze, repeatedly defines his fighting role: he protects Teucer, survives Hector’s attack, defends the ships and the Achaeans, and stands over Patroclus’s body. He begins by killing Simoeisius and Amphius, though Trojan spears prevent him from taking Amphius’s armour. Chosen by lot to meet Hector, he wounds and knocks him down, then ends the combat at nightfall and exchanges gifts, giving Hector a purple-dyed girdle. He aids Teucer at the wall, joins the unsuccessful embassy to Achilles, and condemns Achilles as unforgiving after the mission fails. As Trojan pressure grows, Ajax rescues Ulysses, kills Doryclus, and repeatedly holds back attackers despite fear sent by Jove and volleys of arrows. He aids Menestheus, kills Epicles, presses Hector from the battlement, receives renewed strength from Neptune, and helps establish the Achaean defensive line. In sustained fighting he challenges and repeatedly wounds or repels Hector, kills Archelochus and Laodamas, and exhorts the Achaeans as he leads the defense at the ships. Eventually Trojan darts and Jove’s will overwhelm him; when Hector cuts his spear, he withdraws because he recognizes himself as defenceless. He returns to defend Patroclus with Menelaus, kills Hippothous, and calls for united hand-to-hand resistance. The record closes with athletic contests: he wrestles Ulysses in a closely balanced match and competes against Diomed, his shield being pierced but his body unharmed.

Idomeneus is a grey-haired Achaean warrior, captain and ruler of the Cretans, son of Deucalion, and trusted comrade of Meriones. He leads the Cretans in battle with his ox-hide and bronze round shield. After seeing Machaon wounded, he tells Nestor to carry him away because a physician is highly valuable. Urged by Neptune, he returns to battle, joins Meriones, attacks the weak left wing, rallies the Danaans, panics the Trojans, kills Erymas, Othryoneus, Asius, and Alcathous, and fights on despite fatigue and missiles.

Priam is the old king of Troy and Ilius, ruler of the Trojans, a descendant of Dardanus and son of Laomedon. He is father to many sons, fifty in all, including Hector, Deiphobus, Democoon, and Alexandrus (Paris), and Hector is his bravest son and guardian of the city. As the Achaeans attack his city, Priam appears among the Trojans at the gates, agrees to swear a covenant on the plain, asks Helen about the leading Achaean warriors, and leaves before he can watch his son fight. He later watches Achilles from a tower, opens Troy’s gates to the fleeing Trojans, and tries to keep Achilles out. When Achilles approaches, Priam begs Hector to return within the city, fearing Hector’s death, Troy’s destruction, and dishonour to his own old body. After Hector is killed, Priam mourns, tries to go alone to the Achaeans, and plans to appeal to Achilles through Peleus. Ordered by Iris to ransom Hector, he defies Hecuba’s warnings, takes treasure and ransom gifts in his chariot with Idaeus, and goes to Achilles’ ships. In Achilles’ tent he clasps and kisses Achilles’ hands, begs for Hector’s body, and weeps with him. Priam gives the ransom, receives Hector’s body, obtains nine days for mourning and funeral preparations, returns to Troy, and directs the burial rites.

The Myrmidons are warriors, famed horsemen, and Achilles’s trusted companions, brought to Troy in fifty ships. Led by Achilles and, at key moments, by Patroclus, they arm in ordered companies, surge from the ships, attack the Trojans, and help drive them from the fleet. They fight beside the Achaeans over Sarpedon’s body, losing Epeigeus and carrying Sarpedon’s armour away. After Patroclus dies, they mourn with Achilles, tend his body, accompany him to the pyre, and follow Achilles’s funeral orders.
Pylos, led by Nestor, sends forces from Pylos, Arene, and neighboring places, contributing ninety ships.

Troy, also called Ilius, is Priam’s city and the stronghold of the Trojans. It has walls, the Scaean and Dardanian gates, the sacred Pergamus sanctuary, and rich plains; before it stand Batieia and the battlefield where Sarpedon dies. Priam rules it, while Hector is its chief guardian, defending its gates, battlements, wives, children, and people alongside the Trojans and numerous allies. From the beginning, Troy is the object of the Achaeans’ campaign: Agamemnon expects it to be taken, and a prophecy says it will fall in the tenth year. Alexandrus’s conflict endangers the city and its children, while Juno desires its destruction despite Jove’s respect for Troy, Priam, and their people. The war repeatedly moves between the city, its walls, and the Achaean ships. Trojans sally out to fight, may retreat within the walls, and seek divine protection in Pergamus; their women pray to Minerva. The city remains untaken through severe pressure. Hector rejects advice to withdraw behind its walls, and Patroclus nearly takes Troy before Apollo drives him back. Achilles then drives defenders toward the city, seeks to hasten its destruction, and pursues Hector around its walls. When Hector is forced to fight and dies, the gates and walls have failed to save Troy’s protector. The city receives his body in widespread mourning. Hecuba, Priam, and the people fear that Troy will eventually be razed and overthrown, now deprived of Hector, though these records do not report its capture.

Ilius, also called Troy, is the strong city and citadel of the Trojans, Priam, and Priam’s people. It is protected and respected by Jove, yet its fate is repeatedly threatened: Juno is allowed to seek its destruction, and Agamemnon, Hector, and others foresee that Ilius, Priam, and the Trojan people will be laid low. Hector is its chief guardian and defender. Early in the fighting, Trojans retreat into the city, Hector enters it to seek support, and its women pray in Minerva’s temple on the acropolis for its safety. Hector returns there for Trojan council, while its walls, houses, and watchfires become part of its defense. The Achaeans have failed to take Ilius, whose former wealth is remembered, but they seek to sack it. As losses mount, Hector declares it undone; several gods desire its destruction, though Jove’s protection remains contested. The Trojans try to bring Patroclus’s body into Ilius, and later the Achaeans prepare to fight against it. Achilles drives the Trojans toward its citadel, while Apollo protects the city and Agenor stands before its walls. The Trojans withdraw within Ilius as Achilles is drawn away, then Hector is pursued beneath its wall and killed. Its people mourn, and all of frowning Ilius seems smirched with fire. In the end, the city remains hated by Juno, Neptune, and Jove’s grey-eyed daughter because of Alexandrus’s choice, while Priam leaves it to ransom Hector’s body and his family returns to it from the plain.

Olympus is a snowy, heavenly, many-delled mountain and divine dwelling: the home of the gods and immortals, with mansions, summits, topmost ridges, an assembly, and Jove’s bronze-floored mansion. It is chiefly the seat of Jove, who sits on its highest ridges or golden throne, convenes councils, watches Troy and battle, directs the gods, and sends commands. Thetis petitions him there, and Olympus reels when he confirms his promise or enters its assembly; Juno also makes it quake in rage. From its summits Minerva descends to obey Jove, while Juno looks down and later departs to pursue her deception. Gods flee or return there after conflict: Mars arrives wounded, and Diana reaches Jove’s mansion weeping. During battle, Jove remains on Olympus as other gods go among Trojans and Achaeans, and it receives defeated gods. At the end, the gods assemble there again as Jove instructs Thetis and Iris, and Iris carries divine commands to Priam.
Chryse is Apollo's sacred harbour, where Ulysses returns Chryseis to Chryses and a hecatomb ends Apollo's pestilence.

Argos, an Achaean homeland and country, sends eighty ships under Diomed, Sthenelus, and Euryalus, while Pelasgic Argos is separately listed under Achilles. Later Agamemnon proposes returning to Argos and honoring Achilles there through marriage.

is_home_of Achilles [his homeland] Phthia is Achilles's homeland, where his father is said to be grieving and growing old. Achilles imagines Patroclus returning there with his son and speaks of taking Briseis there.

Hades is both a god, lord of the dead and noble steeds, and the dark house and realm of the dead. It contains Patroclus's spirit, barred from those beyond the river, while Achilles is destined to die beneath Troy's walls.

l: the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, The Iliad
s: The quarrel is a conflict between Agamemnon and Achilles. It begins over prizes, as Agamemnon refuses to release Chryseis without compensation and threatens, then takes, Briseis. Minerva prevents violence; Achilles withdraws from fighting. Later Achilles sets aside anger, while Agamemnon blames divine Folly and offers amends.

l: Achilles' withdrawal from the war, The Iliad
s: Achilles' withdrawal from the Trojan War follows his quarrel with Agamemnon and the taking of Briseis. He returns with Patroclus and his company to his tents and ships, refuses to fight for the Achaeans, and predicts they will seek him vainly in suffering. He then prepares to sail his provisioned ships toward Phthia, if granted fair passage.

l: plague among the Achaeans, The Iliad
s: A plague sent by Apollo after Agamemnon dishonours Chryses strikes the Achaeans for nine days, killing people and animals, until they purify themselves, sacrifice, and return Chryseis to appease Apollo.

Achilles’ anger is rage caused by Agamemnon’s seizure of Briseis, which Achilles sees as dishonor and insult. Directed chiefly against Agamemnon, it nearly drives Achilles to kill him before Minerva restrains him. Achilles withdraws from assembly and battle, keeps his people by the ships and seashore, and brings countless ills upon the Achaeans, who are to regret losing him from the fighting. Agamemnon’s embassy offers gifts, promises, and appeals, but neither these nor Phoenix and Ajax can move Achilles while the anger remains fixed. After Patroclus’s death, Achilles says his anger against Agamemnon is over and renounces it, compelled to return to battle.

Apollo sends a pestilence against the Achaeans after Agamemnon dishonors Apollo’s priest and Chryses prays. For nine days Apollo’s arrows cause widespread death. Calchas says it will continue until Chryseis is returned and a holy hecatomb is sent; it ends after Chryses receives her and sacrifices and prays.

l: Chryseis' release and return to Chryses, The Iliad
s: Chryseis’ release is Agamemnon’s response to Apollo’s plague: after Calchas explains the cause, Ulysses takes her and a holy hecatomb by ship to Chryses at Chryse.

l: the sacrifice to Apollo, The Iliad
s: includes the hecatomb [with prayer, offerings, and a feast] The sacrifice to Apollo is conducted at Chryse after Chryseis is returned. Chryses and the Achaeans pray, burn the thigh-bones, feast, and hymn Apollo, after which the pestilence is stopped.

The Trojan War is a war at Troy, before Ilius, between the Achaeans, also called Danaans and Argives, and the Trojans and their allies. It is fought for Helen, according to Achilles, and brings the Achaeans to attack Trojan cities for prizes and to seek satisfaction for Agamemnon and Menelaus. It lasts nine years before Troy is taken in the tenth. The conflict is shaped above all by the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles. Achilles says he has no personal grievance against the Trojans, yet has taken twelve cities by sea and eleven around Troy by land without adequate reward. When he withdraws, the war is endangered; Jove promises Trojan success until the Achaeans make amends. By the ninth year, the Achaeans are far from home, their ships and equipment decaying, but Agamemnon orders another day of battle. Both sides muster commanders, allies, ships, and formations. After an agreement following the fight between Menelaus and Alexandrus is broken by Pandarus’s attack on Menelaus, combat resumes. The Achaeans attack while the Trojans defend their city. Hector leads Trojan preparations to strike at the Achaean ships, and Hector’s attacks inflict severe losses, leaving Achaean leaders fearful and prompting watches and reconnaissance. Gods debate and intervene: Juno and Minerva seek to join the fighting, Jove restrains them, and later divine intervention prevents Troy’s immediate capture. Repeated fighting brings deaths, grief, and slaughter. Patroclus’s death returns Achilles to battle, where his renewed assault drives the Trojans toward Ilius and becomes immensely destructive. After Achilles kills Hector, Hector’s wife fears labour and sorrow for Astyanax, while Achilles considers an immediate attack on Troy. The war continues amid mourning: Priam’s sons have died, yet Priam and Achilles briefly set aside the conflict to grieve. Ultimately, after nine years of warfare, Troy is taken in the tenth.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad
s: The ships of the Achaeans are a military fleet for the Trojan War, part of the Achaean camp and stationed in rows on the shore by the broad Hellespont, opposite the Trojan city near the Scaean gates. They transport and hold the Danaan contingents, whose ships are counted from two under Guneus to a hundred under Agamemnon; after nine years, their timbers and tackling are deteriorated. Ulysses’ ship stands centrally in the line, between the ships of Ajax and Achilles, while Achilles’ ships remain apart from the fighting. The fleet matters above all as the Achaeans’ refuge, defensive position, and threatened means of escape. When the army thinks of returning home, it rushes toward the ships, though Minerva and Ulysses stop it from launching them. As Hector and the Trojans advance, they seek to reach, capture, and burn the ships, while the Achaeans repeatedly retreat to, rally at, and defend them. Their threatened destruction prompts the embassy to Achilles; commanders inspect guards, conduct scouting, and debate whether to put the ships offshore, a plan Ulysses rejects as harmful to morale. The battle increasingly closes around the fleet. Trojans breach the wall and gates, fight beside and beneath the ships, and drive the Achaeans back from the first row. Defenders use pikes from the decks, fight among the ships and tents, and prevent fire from taking hold despite heavy losses. The ships also frame Achilles’ withdrawal and return to concern: he remains beside them while the army suffers, Patroclus moves among them, and later Patroclus’s body is contested and recovered near them. At the end, Achilles says Patroclus will receive funeral rites at the ships.
A woman awarded to Achilles as a war prize, she is seized by Agamemnon, prompting Achilles to appeal to Thetis and withdraw from battle.
A sacrifice offered to Apollo at Chryse, sent with Chryseis, arranged around the altar, sacrificed, roasted, eaten, and accompanied by song and prayer.

The gods are a divine assembly living and meeting with Jove on Olympus, under his overwhelming authority. They return there after feasting among the Ethiopians, stand before Jove amid his quarrel with Juno, then feast, hear Apollo and the Muses, and retire. As the conflict unfolds, they assemble to hear Jove forbid aid to either side, fearfully fall silent, yet remain divided: Minerva and Juno pity the Danaans, while they reject Trojan sacrifices because they hate Ilius, Priam, and his people.

Vulcan is a lame god of fire, a cunning divine workman of heaven and Olympus, and Juno’s son. He has a house with golden handmaids, is Charis’s husband, and was cared for by Thetis and Eurynome for nine years after his fall. His work includes Diomed’s cuirass, tripods, a golden seat for Sleep, and Achilles’ armor. When Thetis asks, he remembers her care and forges Achilles a shield, breastplate, helmet, and greaves. Later, obeying Juno, he burns the plain and Xanthus until Juno orders him to stop.

The gods are immortal, blessed beings subject to Jove, who is stronger than the other immortals and sits with them. They receive concern over mortal affairs but are described as not subject to mortal care; Achilles contrasts their freedom from care with humanity’s mixed fortunes from Jove. They first sit beside Jove and marvel at the Achaeans’ work while Neptune objects to a wall built without offerings. At Jove’s house they are troubled by his plans, and Minerva restrains Mars from provoking Jove’s punishment. They then divide between Achaeans and Trojans, intensify battle with divine signs, and later mostly watch. Some directly aid or oppose fighters, including Achilles, the Trojans, and Xanthus. Their divided counsels become a quarrel and battle, ending with departures to Olympus. Finally, they pity and protect Hector’s corpse, debate its treatment, and support Jove’s ransom decision, though some continue to hate Ilius and its people.
contains Thetis [in its depths] Achilles weeps and prays beside the hoar sea. Thetis rises from its depths to comfort him and later returns to it after securing Jove's promise.

l: Agamemnon's insult and seizure of Achilles' prize, The Iliad
s: Agamemnon dishonours Achilles by taking the woman awarded to him, a seizure Achilles calls deception and a bitter wrong. Achilles withdraws, asks Thetis for divine compensation, and refuses to fight until his honour is restored; Jove agrees to aid the Trojans until the Achaeans restore it.

l: the promise of Jove, The Iliad
s: concerns the Trojans [granting them victory until Achilles is honoured] The promise of Jove is made to Thetis after she clasps his knees and asks him to help Achilles. Jove confirms it by inclining his head and promises victory to the Trojans until the Achaeans give Achilles his due.

The Muses are Olympian goddesses, daughters of Jove, dwelling on Olympus and singing sweetly at the gods' banquet; invoked to recount Danaans, they see all things and punish Thamyris by removing his song.
A dream sent by Jove, appearing as Nestor, visits Agamemnon and falsely tells him to arm the Achaeans because Troy will fall, leaving him certain of victory that day.

Danaans are the Greek forces assembled for the Trojan War: the Achaeans, Argives, and Greek army besieging Troy. They are warriors with ships and tents, organized by regional contingents, chiefs, territories, and ships. Their host crosses the plain toward the city in a movement heavy enough to make the earth groan. They fight Trojans and gods fighting mortals, serve Mars, and repeatedly defend their ships and positions. After Agamemnon speaks, they applaud; rallied by him, they advance silently and in order, kill Trojan fighters, and suffer losses. They stand against Trojan attacks but retreat when Mars is with the Trojans. At sunset they slaughter oxen, eat at their tents, obtain wine with bronze, iron, hides, whole heifers, and captives, feast all night, and make wine offerings to Jove before sleeping. Their fortunes worsen as Hector and the Trojans inflict heavy losses; Agamemnon prays for their survival, and Jove grants that his people will live. An embassy seeks Achilles’ help and offers gifts, but he rejects the value of their fighting and tells them to find another way to save their ships and people. They try to hold the wall and battlements, yet flee toward their ships after Hector enters the gates. With the wall broken and the ships threatened, Neptune restores their courage. They form a dense line around the two Ajaxes, exchange armour so their strongest fighters have the best equipment, check Hector, and then attack fiercely. They kill Trojan chieftains, pursue fleeing Trojans, and gain the upper hand. Finally, they defend Patroclus’s body in close formation: driven back at first, they rally around Ajax and fight throughout the day.

The Argives are another name for the Achaeans, the Greek army also called Danaans, assembled against the Trojans. They possess the Achaean ships, which serve as their camp, refuge, and the chief point of danger in the war. Led and counselled by figures including Agamemnon, Ulysses, Nestor, Ajax, and Achilles, they fight to take the Trojan city. They are first stirred by Agamemnon’s proposal to sail home, but Ulysses and Nestor recall them to assembly and persuade them to continue. Agamemnon urges them to attack bravely; they advance with a shout, yet suffer severe losses while Mars aids their enemies. Juno rebukes their loss of courage and restores their spirit. As Jove’s favor turns against them, they retreat toward their ships, rally briefly, and are repeatedly driven back by Hector and the Trojans. Their danger becomes extreme: destruction at the ships is threatened, leaders must remain watchful and united, and the Trojans guard against escape by sea. Though panic occurs, they regroup around Eurypylus and Ajax, fight in order within the wall, defend it against the Lycians, and fiercely protect their ships. Hector nevertheless breaks the gates. Later, Achilles summons the Achaean heroes; they witness his reconciliation with Agamemnon and prepare to fight. After Hector’s death, Achilles calls the Argives his friends, princes, and counsellors and proposes an attack on the city. They also participate in and judge the chariot races. At the end, their ships and camps remain near Achilles as Priam is told to cross the Achaeans’ camp and go to their ships to ransom Hector’s body.

contains Achaeans [when summoned by the criers] The assembly is first convened for the elders at Nestor's ship and then for the whole army. It becomes disorderly when the people rush toward the ships, but Ulysses and the heralds restore silence so that counsel can be heard.

Mercury is a god, slayer of Argus, and divine guide and guardian. With golden sandals and a wand that causes sleep or waking, he escorts Priam and Idaeus safely to Achilles, sleeping the guards, opening the gates, delivering them and the treasure, then returning to Olympus.

Juno and Minerva set out together to help the dying Danaans and confront Hector, but Jove prevents them through Iris’s warning. They return to Olympus and sit apart from Jove, angry at his treatment of them. They agree not to fight directly against his will, though they intend to give the Argives useful advice.

is_held_by Cephallenians [with several neighboring islands] Ithaca is held by the Cephallenians, who also occupy Neritum, Crocylea, Aegilips, Samos, Zacynthus, and nearby mainland. These people bring twelve ships under Ulysses.
Thersites, the ugliest soldier before Troy and a habitual critic of authority, attacks Agamemnon and urges departure until Ulysses rebukes, beats, and silences him.

Helen, a Spartan woman formerly of Lacedaemon and daughter of Jove, is central to the war because the Trojans hold her while the Achaeans fight and many die far from home. Once Menelaus’s wife, she is also Paris’s, or Alexandrus’s, wife after he brought her to Troy; this wrong drives Menelaus’s suffering and revenge. Attended by Aethra and Clymene, she weaves battles fought for her sake. She mourns her former husband, city, parents, and life, identifies Achaean leaders from the tower, reproaches Alexandrus after his defeat, and is forced by Venus to join him. In Paris’s house she condemns herself and him, sympathizes with Hector, and later laments Hector as her kindest brother-in-law. Though Antenor urges her return with her wealth and Agamemnon demands it, Alexandrus refuses to surrender her.

l: prophecy of Troy’s fall, The Iliad
s: foretells Troy [the city falls in the tenth year] At Aulis, Calchas interprets a serpent's killing of eight sparrows and their mother as a sign that the Achaeans will fight for nine years and take Troy in the tenth. Ulysses invokes this prophecy to persuade the Achaeans to remain.

is_proposed_by Agamemnon son of Atreus [as a test of the army’s resolve] Agamemnon proposes that the Achaeans sail back to Argos because Troy has not yet been taken. The army briefly attempts to prepare its ships for the return, but Minerva and Ulysses stop the movement.

l: flight of the Achaeans, The Iliad
s: is_prevented_by Minerva [at Juno’s command] The flight of the Achaeans begins when Agamemnon tests them by urging them to sail home. They rush toward the ships, but Juno sends Minerva to prevent the flight, and Ulysses brings the army back to assembly.

The Achaean army, a host of Achaeans, gathers in confusion but is disciplined by Ulysses and reminded of its oath, labor, and promised victory. Agamemnon orders preparation for battle; chiefs organize its vast, armoured ranks as Minerva strengthens their courage.

The two Ajaxes are an Achaean fighting pair and defensive force, leading foot soldiers, guarding the gates and walls, and urging the Danaans to resist. They act as chief defenders, fighting side by side in a compact formation of spears, shields, helmets, and men. As the Trojan attack intensifies, they rebuke the remiss, rally the defenders, receive Neptune’s encouragement, and check Hector’s advance. They then force through the crowd to rescue Automedon and defend Patroclus's body, protecting Menelaus and Meriones as they carry it away while holding back the pursuing Trojans.

Diomed is an Achaean warrior, chief, and commander of eighty ships from Argos, Tiryns, Hermione, Asine, Troezene, Eionae, Epidaurus, Aegina, and Mases. Son of Tydeus, he is renowned for fierce fighting, though Agamemnon compares him unfavourably with his father; Diomed accepts the rebuke, restrains Sthenelus, and enters battle. Dear to Jove and Minerva according to Nestor, he fights with exceptional fury, panics the Trojans, and continues despite wounds. With Minerva’s protection he wounds Venus and Mars, while Apollo warns him away from Aeneas. He kills Axylus, Calesius, Agelaus, Dolon, Rhesus, twelve Thracian soldiers, Thymbraeus, and others in the Trojan fighting. His conduct also shows restraint and loyalty: when he learns that Glaucus is linked to his father’s house, he refuses to fight him and exchanges armor; when Nestor is endangered, he takes him into his chariot. During the night reconnaissance he volunteers, chooses Ulysses, takes sword, shield, and helmet, prays to Pallas Minerva, captures Dolon, and returns with Ulysses after Minerva’s warning. He attacks Hector repeatedly but retreats when Jove frightens his horses and later withdraws after Alexandrus wounds his foot. Even wounded, he counsels the Achaean leaders to return and encourage the fighters. After battle, he wins the chariot race with Trojan horses taken from Aeneas, supports Euryalus in boxing, and earns a sword and equipment after threatening Ajax in the armor contest.

Jove is the supreme divine ruler: father and sire of gods and men, king of the gods and of Dodona, son of Saturn, lord of counsel, and husband and brother of Juno. From Ida, holding his thunderbolt, he watches and directs the war through Iris, Mercury, Apollo, portents, strength, and divine intervention. He initially favors the Trojans, orders Hector to wait for Agamemnon’s wounding, and promises him power to drive the Achaeans to their ships. Juno seduces him and causes him to sleep, briefly allowing Neptune to help the Achaeans. Jove grants Achilles that Patroclus will repel the battle from the ships but denies Patroclus a safe return. He pities his son Sarpedon yet accepts his death, honors him with bloody rain, shapes the fighting, and has Apollo prepare his body for transport. He gives Achilles’ helmet to Hector, protects Hector’s body, and ultimately hears Priam’s prayer, sends a favorable eagle and Mercury’s escort, and has Hector’s body returned. He also governs fortune and suffering through two urns.

Mars is an immortal, warlike god of war, son of Juno and fathered by Jove, a divine warrior, piercer of shields, and father of Ascalaphus. He possesses gold-bedizened steeds and a sword, and is associated with causing the war over Helen and with battle’s destructive force. Fighting for the Trojans, he destroys many Achaeans, rallies the Trojans in the likeness of Acamas, and covers them with darkness. Minerva enables Diomed to wound him; he cries out, flees to Olympus, complains to Jove, and Paeeon heals him. He later attacks Minerva, but she knocks him down with a stone. Venus leads him away, and Minerva draws him from battle, allowing the Danaans to drive back the Trojans.

Neptune is a god: lord and shaker of the earthquake, ruler of the sea, king of Helice, and holder of the world in his embrace. He is one of Saturn’s three sons, brother to Jove and Hades, with the sea as his allotted realm; though he claims equal honor with Jove, he submits when Jove commands. He has a golden palace at Aegae beneath the sea and a golden chariot drawn by brazen-footed horses. With Phoebus Apollo he built walls for Laomedon, including the wall of Ilius, and he later objects when the Achaeans build a wall and trench without honoring the gods, fearing it will rival their work. Jove permits him to destroy that wall after the Achaeans depart; Neptune will shatter it with his trident, fling it into the sea, and cover the beach with sand. During the fighting he is angered by Jove’s favoring of the Trojans and secretly supports the Achaeans and Danaans. From Samothrace and then from the sea, he uses disguises, including Calchas and an old man, to strengthen, cheer, rally, and lead them; he protects Antilochus, helps bring about Alcathous’s death through Idomeneus, and fights with a terrible flashing sword. When Iris brings Jove’s order, he protests but withdraws beneath the sea. Later he counsels restraint at Jove’s council, rescues Aeneas from Achilles because fate preserves Aeneas and the race of Dardanus, and reassures Achilles against Xanthus. Finally, he challenges Apollo, recalls their service to Laomedon, but does not fight when Apollo refuses.

Scamander is a fair river and river god at Troy, descended from Immortal Jove, brother to Simois, with warm and cold springs and a channel to the sea. Enraged by corpses, it floods Achilles and seeks Simois’s aid, but Vulcan scalds it into submission.
The tents stand near the sea with the sea behind them and contain Patroclus's funeral pyre; after retreating from the ships, the Achaeans defend them resolutely.
A priceless, deathless shaggy-fringed aegis with a Gorgon head and hundred gold tassels; Jove gives it to Apollo, whose stillness allows strikes, but shaking it panics Achaeans.

This is an armed battle between Trojans and Achaeans, arising from Alexandrus carrying Helen away from her husband and homeland. It is prepared through sacrifices, prayers, mustering, and the disposition of chiefs’ men, as Agamemnon urges an immediate attack. At first, both armies hope a single combat will settle the dispute and let them separate, but their ranks instead meet in sustained, bloody fighting of shields and spears. Warriors on both sides are killed as the struggle repeatedly shifts across the plain between Simois and Xanthus. Divine intervention is central: Apollo, Minerva, Mars, Juno, Venus, and others aid, restrain, rescue, or conceal fighters. Diomed’s attacks, including his wounding of Mars, temporarily check Trojan pressure; Apollo restores Aeneas, while Hector repeatedly rallies the Trojans. Agamemnon leads a devastating Achaean advance, but after he is wounded Hector helps reverse the course. The Trojans eventually confine the Achaeans at their ships. Patroclus attacks the Trojans but is killed, marking a major outcome of the fighting. Battle is also depicted on Vulcan’s shield through besieging armies, ambush, slain shepherds, armed hosts, Strife, Riot, and Fate.

is_a assembly [of the Achaean people] The Achaean mustering begins when Agamemnon sends criers to summon the people to assembly. The chiefs choose and marshal their men, while the assembled forces pour from the ships and tents onto the plain.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Iliad
s: Ajax son of Oileus is a swift, impetuous Argive and Achaean warrior who commands the Locrians and their forty ships. Smaller than Ajax son of Telamon and wearing a linen breastplate, he nevertheless excels Hellenes and Achaeans in spear use. In battle he stands continually beside Ajax son of Telamon, while his bow- and sling-armed Locrians remain behind. Recognizing Neptune in Calchas’s likeness, he is stirred to fight, throws at Hector, helps recover Imbrius, and beheads him for Amphimachus. He kills Satnius and Cleobulus, and, when the Trojans flee in panic, kills more than any other through swift pursuit. His speed also leads the running contest until he slips near the finish, loses to Ulysses, and says Minerva favored Ulysses. He is Medon’s brother.

is_held_by Athenians [strong city] Athens is held by the people of Erechtheus and sends fifty ships under Menestheus. The Athenian contingent is stationed beside the ships brought from Salamis by Ajax son of Telamon.
Euryalus, Mecisteus's champion-boxer son, alone challenges Epeus, is knocked down, and is led away by comrades bleeding, disoriented, and unconscious.
is_led_by Agamemnon [king; son of Atreus] Mycenae, together with Corinth, Cleonae, and other surrounding lands, sends a hundred ships. These forces are commanded by Agamemnon.
Sparta and surrounding Lacedaemonian settlements send sixty ships under Menelaus, their contingent drawn up apart from the others.

Meriones is a brave, valorous Achaean warrior and the stalwart squire of Idomeneus, serving him in battle and commanding Cretan rear battalions. He fights prominently, breaks his spear on Deiphobus’s shield, rearms, and leads with Idomeneus toward the left wing. He wounds Deiphobus, kills Acamas, Adamas, and Harpalion, and proves skilled beyond battle: he finishes fourth in chariot racing, wins the archery contest and ten axes, and receives a spear in the javelin contest.
is_son_of Hercules Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, challenges Sarpedon and boasts of his father's destruction of Ilius. He wounds Sarpedon in the thigh but is struck through the throat and dies.

Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, is a brave Achaean warrior and prince. During fighting, he helps Ajax by killing Apisaon and taking his armour. Alexandrus wounds his right thigh with an arrow, forcing him from battle; he urges defense of Ajax, limps to Ulysses’ ships, and receives treatment from Patroclus.
Eumelus, son of Admetus and an excellent horseman, leads a chariot race until Minerva breaks his yoke; injured and last, he receives Achilles’ bronze breastplate.

Machaon, son of Aesculapius, is a physician and surgeon valued by the army. Agamemnon summons him to treat Menelaus: he removes an arrow and applies soothing drugs given by Chiron to Aesculapius. Later Alexandrus wounds Machaon in the right shoulder with a triple-barbed arrow. Nestor carries him by chariot toward the ships, where Machaon rests in Nestor’s tent needing healing himself.

Iris is a winged, golden-winged, fleet messenger goddess who serves Jove and the gods, moving as swiftly as the wind. She carries commands that shape the Trojan war: warning the Trojans while disguised as Polites, directing Hector’s response to Agamemnon, ordering Neptune to withdraw, secretly urging Achilles to appear and drive back the Trojans, and conveying Jove’s instructions to Thetis and Priam about Hector’s ransom. Though usually Jove’s messenger, she also secretly delivers Juno’s message without Jove’s knowledge. Her work ends with Priam’s ransom mission, which she escorts by Jove’s command.

Aeneas is a Trojan warrior, prince, and leader: son of Anchises and Venus, loved by Venus, and a mainstay of the Trojans and Lycians in fighting and counsel. He is among the best Trojan warriors with Hector, leads the Dardanians, owns Trojan horses, and is fated, with his descendants, to reign over the Trojans. Although aggrieved because Priam son of Dardanus did not give him his due honour, he repeatedly serves the Trojan cause. He joins Pandarus against Diomed, drives their chariot, and is struck in the hip by a stone. Near death, he is carried from battle by Venus, hidden by Apollo, healed at Pergamus by Latona and Diana, and returns to kill Crethon and Orsilochus. He is urged by Helenus to rally the Trojans, fights with Deiphobus against Idomeneus's group, and kills Aphareus. Later he joins Hector in pursuing the retreating Achaeans and seeking Achilles' horses. Finally, encouraged by Apollo, he confronts Achilles, declares his ancestry, casts a spear, and lifts a stone; Neptune rescues him and tells him to avoid Achilles until Achilles is dead. His course is marked by command, battle, wounds, divine protection, recovery, and survival.

Venus is a goddess, daughter of Jove/Jupiter and Dione, associated with charms through her girdle and with Alexandrus’s love-tricks. She repeatedly protects those she favors: she rescues Alexandrus from Menelaus, breaks his helmet strap, hides him in darkness, carries him to his bedchamber, and compels Helen to join him. She loves Aeneas as her son and rescues him from battle beneath her garment, but Diomed wounds her hand and she leaves Aeneas to Apollo; Iris brings her to Olympus, where Dione heals her. Though Jove judges her not a warrior, she aids Trojans, protects Hector’s body, helps Mars, and later tries to lead the wounded Mars away before Minerva strikes her down. She also lends Juno her girdle of love, desire, and charm before returning to Jupiter’s house.

Pandarus, Lycaon’s son from Zelea and Lycia, is a Trojan archer whose chief weapon is an ibex-horn bow. Persuaded by Minerva disguised as Laodocus, he prays to Lycian Apollo and shoots Menelaus with an unused winged arrow.

Lycaon, son of Priam and Laothoe, is captured and ransomed from Lemnos before fleeing Xanthus. He begs Achilles for mercy, recalling their past encounter, but Achilles kills him over Patroclus’s death and casts him into the river.
The Thracians are a Trojan-allied people led by Rhesus son of Eioneus, camped apart at the far end with armour and horses nearby; while sleeping, Diomed kills Rhesus and twelve soldiers.

Sarpedon is a Lycian prince, king, captain, and Jove’s son, dearly loved by Jove and counted the best of the allied captains. He leads the Lycians from their distant land beside the Xanthus with Glaucus, his trusted comrade and brother, and insists that their honors require them to fight in the forefront. Having left wife, infant son, and wealth in Lycia, he rebukes Hector and fights for Troy. He kills Tlepolemus but is wounded in the left thigh, carried away, and revived. Later he leads the assault on the Achaean wall, kills Alcmaon, and tears down a battlement to make a breach. At the end, after reproving fleeing Lycians, he confronts Patroclus, is struck near the heart, and dies on the plain of Troy, calling on Glaucus to rally the Lycians and protect his armour.

Glaucus is a Lycian warrior and captain of noble lineage, son of Hippolochus and descended from Bellerophon. He leads the Lycians with his brother Sarpedon, accepting Sarpedon’s call to fight at the front. He tells Diomed his lineage, recognizes old ties of friendship, and exchanges his golden armor for Diomed’s less valuable bronze armor. Wounded by Teucer’s arrow, he withdraws, but after Sarpedon’s death he prays to Apollo, who heals and strengthens him. Glaucus then rallies Lycian and Trojan leaders to defend Sarpedon’s body, rebukes Hector for failing Sarpedon, and threatens that the Lycians will leave Troy unless the Trojans recover Patroclus’s body.

The Lycians are a warrior people from Xanthus, situated in the Trojan camp and fighting for Troy. Led chiefly by Sarpedon, with Glaucus and Hector also guiding them, they suffer heavy losses against Ulysses, defend the wall beside Hector, and follow him through a breach. They flee, regroup at Sarpedon’s rebuke, and fight to defend him after his death, but retreat when they see their king dead.

threatens Troy [massive army crossing the plain] The Achaeans’ advance is so vast that Iris compares them to leaves or the sands of the sea. Their movement across the plain makes the earth groan, and their approach prompts the Trojans to arm and organize.

Briseis’s loss is the cause of Achilles’ continuing grief and withdrawal from the fighting. She had been taken by Achilles after the sack of Lyrnessus and Thebe, but Agamemnon’s quarrel with him leaves her loss at the center of his anger.

Alexandrus, also called Paris, is a Trojan champion, archer, and Helen’s husband, associated with a lyre. He first comes forward for single combat with Menelaus but retreats in fear; after Hector rebukes him, he proposes a fight over Helen and her wealth. Menelaus defeats him, and Venus rescues him. His allies hate him as they hate death and would not hide him. Later he is found at home tending his armor while fighting continues, is again rebuked by Hector, arms himself, and follows him toward battle. He shoots Diomed in the foot and wounds Machaon and Eurypylus. On the left wing he encourages his men, fights the Danaans, reports comrades’ losses and wounds, and vows to follow Hector as far as his strength allows.
Scaean gates open to shelter fleeing Trojans, then Priam closes them against Achilles; Hector remains there before fleeing Achilles and foretells Paris and Apollo will kill Achilles there.

l: single combat between Paris and Menelaus, The Iliad
s: A combat for Helen and her wealth is arranged, with peace promised to the loser; Menelaus gains advantage over Alexandrus until Venus rescues him.

l: the covenant of peace, The Iliad
s: The covenant of peace is an agreement between Trojans and Achaeans: they lay down arms, accept the victor's claim to Helen and her wealth, with Achaeans returning home and Trojans remaining in Troy. Leaders swear and seal it with sacrifices, but Venus removes Alexandrus and Pandarus attacks Menelaus, violating it.

is_caused_by Menelaus [in the single combat] Paris's spear fails to pierce Menelaus's shield, while Menelaus's spear passes through Paris's shield and cuirass. Menelaus then breaks his sword against Paris's helmet and captures him by the helmet plume before Venus intervenes.

l: Paris's rescue by Venus, The Iliad
s: In Troy, Venus saves Paris after his defeat, carries him to his bedchamber, and brings Helen to him despite her refusal.
The allies, in the city with the Trojans, sleep instead of keeping watch, leaving the camp’s guard to the Trojans because their wives and children are absent.
is_with Menelaus The victory was declared to have been with Menelaus.
serves_as testimony for posterity [among those that shall be born hereafter] Agamemnon called for a fine to be paid as agreed, as a testimony among those born thereafter.

wounds Menelaus [passing through his belts and cuirass and grazing his skin] The arrow Pandarus fires passes through Menelaus’s outer belt, cuirass, and inner belt before grazing his skin. Minerva diverts it from a mortal part, and Machaon later removes it.

is_between Trojans [and Achaeans as an alternative to renewed war] Jove considers making peace so that Menelaus can take Helen back while Troy remains inhabited. Juno and Minerva reject this outcome and work to renew the conflict.

l: Pandarus’s attack on Menelaus, The Iliad
s: violates oaths [by wounding Menelaus] Pandarus’s attack is prompted by Minerva, who promises him honor and Trojan gratitude if he shoots Menelaus. The shot violates the oaths but fails to kill Menelaus because Minerva diverts the arrow.

is_treated_by Machaon [with extraction of the arrow and soothing drugs] Menelaus’s wound bleeds after the arrow passes through his belts and cuirass, causing Agamemnon and the surrounding Achaeans to fear for him. Machaon removes the arrow and treats the injury with soothing drugs.

l: the destruction of Troy, The Iliad
s: The destruction of Troy is a foreseen, impending sack by the Achaeans, involving fire and the city’s people. Juno intends it as punishment for Trojan treachery, and Jove permits her purpose despite former respect for Ilius. As Achilles assaults, Xanthus expects Troy to burn and will not aid the Trojans.

Antilochus is Nestor’s son, an Achaean warrior, and a notably swift young runner, protected by Neptune in battle. He fights prominently in the foremost ranks, killing Echepolus, Atymnius, Asius’s charioteer, Thoon, and Melanippus; he also helps defend Hypsenor’s body, captures horses from the Trojans, and withdraws when Hector attacks. After Menelaus tells him that Patroclus has fallen and Achilles’ armour has been taken, grief first silences him, but he gives his armour to Laodocus and runs to the ships with the news for Achilles. In the chariot race, he dangerously passes Menelaus with his slow Pylos-bred horses, admits his fault, and offers Menelaus the mare before receiving it back. He later places last in the footrace, jokes about seniority, and gains extra gold from Achilles.
Agenor, valiant son of Antenor, kills Elephenor, defends Ilius, and bravely faces Achilles; after his spear fails, Apollo hides and removes him from battle.

l: breaking of the oaths, The Iliad
s: causes war [by the Trojans’ first attack] Agamemnon and Idomeneus say that the Trojans broke their covenants and oaths first by attacking the Achaeans. They therefore declare that death and destruction should befall the Trojans.
Pallas Minerva, a goddess and daughter of Jove, aids Diomed by giving courage, strength, and clear sight; she directs battle, removes Mars, and permits Diomed to wound Venus.
Diana, Jove’s daughter and Apollo’s sister, is a goddess huntress and patron of wild beasts. Armed with her bow, she challenges Juno, is beaten, loses her arrows, and flees weeping to Olympus.

is_home_of Sarpedon [his rich native land] Lycia is Sarpedon’s rich homeland, where Jove orders Apollo, Death, and Sleep to take him after his death. Sarpedon’s brothers and kinsmen are expected to bury him there with a mound and pillar.

l: Diomed’s wounding by Pandarus, The Iliad
s: is_a wounding [Diomed is wounded in the shoulder by Pandarus’s arrow and spear] Pandarus wounds Diomed in the shoulder with an arrow that pierces his cuirass, but Sthenelus removes it. Pandarus later strikes Diomed’s shield and breastplate with a spear, yet Diomed remains unharmed enough to kill him.

is_a death [caused by Diomed] Diomed kills Pandarus by throwing a spear that Minerva guides into his face near the eye. The spear passes through his teeth and tongue, and Pandarus falls dead from the chariot.

is_a wounding [Aeneas is wounded in the hip by Diomed] Diomed wounds Aeneas by striking him in the hip with a massive stone. The blow crushes the joint, breaks the sinews, and leaves Aeneas on his knees with darkness covering his eyes.

l: Venus’s rescue of Aeneas, The Iliad
s: is_a rescue [Venus carries Aeneas out of battle] Venus sees Aeneas in danger and throws her arms around him, shielding him with her garment. She carries him out of the fight, but Apollo ultimately takes him and conceals him in a cloud.

l: Venus’s wounding by Diomed, The Iliad
s: Venus’s wounding is an event in which Diomed, permitted by Minerva to fight her, pursues Venus as she rescues Aeneas and pierces her hand near the wrist through her robe. Ichor flows, Venus drops Aeneas, and Dione cleans the wound, ending her pain.

l: Mars's intervention in the battle, The Iliad
s: supports Trojans [by covering them in darkness and encouraging them] Mars enters the battle at Apollo's request, disguised as Acamas. He rallies the Trojans, covers them with darkness, and causes the Danaans to retreat while keeping their faces turned toward the enemy.
Tlepolemus and Sarpedon trade insults and simultaneous spear throws; Sarpedon fatally wounds Tlepolemus’s throat, while Tlepolemus wounds Sarpedon’s thigh before he is carried away alive.

Helenus, Priam’s son and wisest augur, is a leading Trojan and Lycian in battle and counsel. Wounded in the hand but alive, he tells Hector and Aeneas to rally Trojans and seek Minerva’s protection through offerings.

is_dangerous_to mortals [mortals cannot hold their own with immortals] The unit presents mortals confronting and wounding gods: Diomed wounds Venus and challenges Apollo, while Apollo warns that mortals cannot match immortals. Dione also recalls earlier cases in which Mars, Juno, and Hades suffered injuries from mortals.

l: divine intervention in the battle, The Iliad
s: Juno and Minerva enter the fighting directly, encourage the Argives, and assist Diomed against Mars. Minerva conceals herself with the helmet of Hades, deflects Mars's spear, and guides Diomed's spear into him.

is_caused_by Diomed [with Minerva's assistance] Diomed wounds Mars in the stomach after Minerva deflects Mars's attack and guides Diomed's spear. Mars cries out, flees to Olympus, and is healed by Paeeon with pain-killing herbs.

Andromache, daughter of Eetion and born and raised in Thebes, is Hector’s wife and the mother of his child. At the Scaean gates she meets Hector with their child, recalls Achilles’ killing of her father and brothers, and begs Hector not to leave, fearing widowhood and captivity if Troy falls. After Hector’s death, she first prepares his bath, then sees his body dragged away, faints, and mourns for herself and their child. She leads Hector’s lamentation, grieving her husband and fearing the future.

Teucer is an Achaean archer, king, son of Telamon, and half-brother of Ajax son of Telamon. Known for a mighty bow given by Apollo, he also carries a four-hide shield and bronze-shod spear and can fight hand-to-hand. Fighting beside and behind Ajax’s shield, he kills several Trojans, including Gorgythion, Archeptolemus, and Cleitus, while repeatedly aiming at Hector. He wounds Glaucus at the wall and strikes Hector’s shield-band, but Hector later disables his arm with a stone, forcing him to drop his bow; Jove also breaks its string. Teucer then takes spear and shield to fight with Ajax. In an archery contest against Meriones, he cuts the pigeon’s tether and wins the single-edged axes.

The armor contest pits Ajax son of Telamon and Diomed in a shared-armor fight to first blood. Neither wins decisively, so Achilles divides the prizes: Diomed receives the Thracian sword and both contestants share the armor.
Astyanax, Hector’s infant son, was cherished and well provided for, named for Hector’s defense of Troy; after Hector’s death, his mother fears loss of lands, exclusion, hardship, and sorrow.

Hecuba is Priam’s wife and Hector’s mother, defined above all by grief and fear for her family. When Hector is dishonoured, she tears her hair, casts off her veil, leads Trojan lamentation, and mourns him as Troy’s strength. She fears Priam’s ransom journey to Achilles and urges him to stay, but ultimately supports him with wine and prayer. She continues mourning Hector, recalling the suffering of her other sons.

l: single combat between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad
s: is_a single combat [between opposing champions] Diomed and Glaucus meet between the opposing hosts and prepare to fight. Their combat ends without violence when they discover their inherited ties of hospitality and decide to avoid one another’s spears.

l: exchange of armor between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad
s: is_a exchange of armor [between hereditary friends] Diomed and Glaucus exchange armor so that everyone present will know of the old ties between their families. Glaucus gives golden armor valued at a hundred head of cattle and receives bronze armor valued at nine.

l: friendship between Diomed and Glaucus, The Iliad
s: is_a hereditary friendship [sealed by exchanged armor] Diomed and Glaucus establish friendship after learning that Oeneus once entertained Bellerophon. They pledge to be hosts to one another in Argos and Lycia and to avoid fighting each other even during a general engagement.

l: Hector’s appeal to the Trojans, The Iliad
s: is_a call for prayer and offerings [for the safety of Troy] Hector directs his mother and the matrons to pray to Minerva and offer the finest robe and twelve unyoked heifers. The prayer asks Minerva to pity Troy and keep Diomed away from the city, but Minerva does not grant it.

l: Hector and Andromache’s parting, The Iliad
s: is_a farewell between husband and wife [under threat of death and captivity] Hector and Andromache part at the city wall after she begs him to protect her and their child by staying. Hector says that honor and duty require him to fight, comforts her with the thought that no one dies before the appointed time, and returns to battle while she goes home mourning.

is_a enslavement after Troy’s fall [foreseen as a possible fate] Hector foresees that Andromache may be taken captive if the Achaeans destroy Ilius. He imagines her being carried weeping to Argos, forced to weave or fetch water, and treated brutally by a mistress or taskmaster.
Hector and Andromache’s beloved male infant, named Scamandrius by Hector and Astyanax by the people, fears Hector’s armor; Hector comforts him and prays he will become Ilius’s strong, renowned ruler.

Peleus is a mortal, aged ruler of the Myrmidons, their counsellor and orator, and father and former adviser of Achilles. Blessed with prosperity, immortal horses, and Thetis as his goddess wife, he gives the horses and counsel to Achilles and welcomes Phoenix as a son. In old age, his only royal child Achilles is doomed to die and cannot care for him.

l: single combat between Hector and Ajax, The Iliad
